parsed_answer.content:
Gathering requirements for a system design problem is the foundational first phase of architectural engineering. It bridges the gap between vague business objectives and concrete technical specifications. When presented with an open-ended architecture challenge during a technical evaluation or in a production-bound enterprise design session, jumping straight into database schemas or technology choices is a catastrophic anti-pattern. Instead, a senior software engineer must systematically dissect the problem space by categorizing requirements into functional and non-functional buckets, while ruthlessly establishing scale estimations and constraints.

Functional requirements dictate what the system must do—its features, user workflows, and core APIs. Non-functional requirements (NFRs), on the other hand, define how the system must perform, encompassing scalability, availability, latency constraints, durability, and consistency models. Neglecting either side leads to over-engineering or catastrophic system failure under load. Furthermore, clarifying out-of-scope items prevents scope creep and allows the engineering team to focus architectural real estate entirely on the core bottlenecks of the problem.

rows: What are the core use cases? Who are the primary actors? What data is being read or written?
Defines API contracts, data models, domain boundaries, and synchronous vs. asynchronous workflows.
What is the Daily Active Users (DAU) count? Peak-to-average load ratio? Read/Write ratio?
Drives capacity planning, sharding strategies, caching tiers, and auto-scaling group thresholds.
What is the acceptable p99 latency? Is five-nines (99.999%) availability required?
Influences synchronous blocking calls, multi-region replication, failover strategies, and circuit breakers.
Can we tolerate eventual consistency? Is zero data loss mandatory on write?
Determines database engine selection (ACID vs. BASE), replication lags, and write-ahead logging configs.

items: Calculate back-of-the-envelope estimations early: Translate DAU into Queries Per Second (QPS) for both reads and writes to immediately identify whether a single database node or a distributed cluster is required.
Explicitly define data retention policies and storage growth limits over a 3-to-5-year horizon to account for cold storage migration, archiving, and sharding key selection.

Establish boundary conditions regarding consistency models: forcing strong consistency globally on a high-throughput write system will tank availability, so trade-offs must be negotiated upfront with product stakeholders.

parsed_answer.content: The most common junior trap in system design is asking generic, unstructured questions just to check a box. An elite senior engineer drives the requirement-gathering phase by offering educated assumptions ('Given this is a global ride-sharing app, I assume a read-heavy QPS of around 100k with sub-100ms latency on location updates—does that align with your expectations?'). This showcases domain expertise, saves precious time, and anchors the conversation to realistic production constraints.

title: How do you gather requirements for a system design problem?
